Title: Speech for the Fifth Annual PwC/CBP Central Bank Working Group meeting London
Subtitle: Notes on the Impact of Exchange Rate Volatility on the CNBs Capital
text: 19. 5. 2008 Notes on the Impact of Exchange Rate Volatility on the CNBs Capital Eva Zamrazilova, CNB Board Member Speech for the Fifth Annual PwC/CBP Central Bank Working Group meeting London, 19th - 20th May 2008 In the context of our discussion of the various aspects of central bank independence, I would like to make a few comments on the impact of the exchange rate on the capital of the central bank in the case of the CNB. The issue is highly relevant to the CNB, as it is currently operating with substantially negative own capital. While under normal circumstances a central bank should operate at a profit, the CNB has been incurring considerable losses since 2000. Just to give you an idea, its accumulated loss amounted to CZK 200 bn at the end of 2007, equivalent to roughly 57% of currency in circulation and 6.7% of nominal GDP. The CNBs negative own capital was only slightly lower, at CZK 176 bn. At the same time, it can be said - and this is also generally acknowledged in the literature - that the CNB has so far enjoyed a high level of independence in the legal, operational and management fields, and even a high degree of goal independence. Being a pioneer of inflation targeting in the region, the CNB has set its own inflation targets for the conduct of monetary policy. Nevertheless, its increasing accumulated loss and its negative own capital raise questions about the implied risks to its independence. Not even a central bank can accumulate losses indefinitely. It seems obvious that without the prospect of a turnaround, i.e. repayment of the losses from future profits, the financial independence of the central bank will be severely undermined. At the same time, any government involvement in central bank financing could constrain the bank's operational independence and monetary policy-making. The Causes of the Incurred Losses What are the causes of the incurred losses, and what factors can be expected to produce a turnaround? The Czech economy is an example of a catching-up economy, and the convergence conditions have inevitably affected the structure and evolution of the CNBs balance sheet. As is well known, in the convergence process there is a built-in tendency of real exchange rate appreciation, either through the inflation differential or through nominal exchange rate appreciation. Moreover, the non-zero risk premium plays an important role and the balance sheet of a converging central bank is also as a rule negatively affected by sterilised interventions related to the purchase of foreign exchange reserves. True, the sources of the loss and their relative weight may differ across countries and over time. Previous literature has focused on the consequences of quasi-fiscal operations. In the Czech case, such operations - related to the rescue of the banking sector - were of considerable importance in the second half of the 1990s. Since 2000, however, the dominant factor has proved to be trend appreciation of the nominal exchange rate. The Impact of the Exchange Rate on the CNBs Balance Sheet Let me briefly discuss the impact of the exchange rate on the CNB balance sheet. I should point out that two entirely different exchange rate regimes have been applied since the beginning of the transition in the early 1990s. In the first stage, a fixed exchange rate was chosen as a nominal anchor for macroeconomic stabilisation in the early 1990s. Its fluctuation band was initially rather narrow, at 0.5%, but was later widened to 7.5%. In order to keep the rate within the fluctuation band and to avoid excessive nominal exchange rate appreciation, the CNB was forced to purchase the inflowing capital and at the same time to sterilise the liquidity issued. Roughly half of the current foreign exchange reserves were accumulated during the fixed exchange rate period. In May 1997, the exchange rate regime was switched to a flexible one - a version of managed floating. Nevertheless, a substantial amount has been added to the foreign exchange reserves in this period, too. This mainly reflects episodes of foreign exchange interventions when the CNB was trying to fight strong bouts of appreciation. Real Exchange Rate Appreciation Channels: The Inflation Differential and Nominal Exchange Rate Appreciation With the benefit of hindsight, two different stages of real exchange rate appreciation can be distinguished in the Czech case. Up to 1998, the dominant channel was the inflation differential. Between 1993 and 1998, average annual inflation in the Czech Republic amounted to 11.2%, with the inflation differential vis-a-vis the EU fluctuating between 7 and 9%. On the other hand, there was no sustained nominal exchange rate trend. The average annual nominal appreciation with respect to the DM was virtually zero in this period. Of course, exchange rate volatility was experienced from time to time to a greater or lesser extent, but this had no systematic impact on the balance sheet. Minor balance-sheet losses due to revaluations in 1993, 1996 and 1998 were offset by gains in the preceding or subsequent years. It follows that in this period the exchange rate exhibited no systematic pattern and, accordingly, there was no systematic impact on the CNBs balance sheet. The picture has changed totally since 2000. In 1999, Czech inflation dropped to a mere 2.1%, and it has remained low and relatively stable since then. Unlike in the previous stage, real exchange rate appreciation, i.e. the tendency inherent in the convergence process, has started to materialise via persistent nominal exchange rate appreciation. As a result, the nominal appreciation has affected the CNB balance sheet to a substantial degree. Given the marking-to-market of the foreign exchange reserves, we can conclude that the main reason for the CNBs losses since 2000 has been the exchange rate trend. From the accounting point of view, the losses manifest themselves as revaluation of the foreign exchange reserves. What are the Likely Solutions? The answer must be sought again in the context of the economic convergence process. As this progresses, the factors behind the incurred losses - both the trend real exchange rate appreciation and the risk premium - are likely to fade away. Moreover, with increasing monetisation of the Czech economy the foreign exchange reserve ratio will gradually fall, especially if the CNB no longer engages in massive foreign exchange interventions. Thanks to those arguments it can reasonably be expected that the accumulated losses will be settled out of future profits, without recourse to public budgets and without the operational independence of the CNB and its monetary policy credibility being undermined.

Title: Markets in Crypto-assets Regulation (MiCA) will create a new financial services sector
text: Markets in Crypto-assets Regulation (MiCA) create a new financial services sector Jan Prochazka, CNB Bank Board member Effective State Conference - Partner of the Crypto Industry Senate of the Parliament of the Czech Republic, Prague, 26 April 2023 CNB Bank Board member Jan Prochazka attended the Effective State  Partner of the Crypto Industry conference in the Senate on Wednesday 26 April. In his speech, he spoke about the regulation of crypto-assets in the Czech Republic and the EU. Selected quotes from Jan Prochazka's speech in the Senate Currently, crypto-assets in the Czech Republic are only subject to the rules for the prevention of money laundering and supervision by the Financial Analytical Office (FAU), unless they meet the definition of regulated financial services, which may be the case with electronic money or derivatives, otherwise crypto-assets are not subject to financial regulation or supervision by the CNB. Investors should be aware of this fact and take into account the related risks in their investment decisions, which the CNB continuously draws the CNB's attention to to the public. The CNB considered this to be sufficient and generally did not consider it necessary to regulate crypto-assets as financial services, and therefore did not propose any special national legislation for crypto-assets and related activities in the past, as has been introduced in some EU Member States. At EU level, the definition of tokenized investment securities is still not harmonized, which is thus subject to national regulation in individual Member States. This leads to a situation where in some EU countries, investment tokens are considered investment securities and are subject to regulation by default Therefore, the CNB has long demanded that the technological neutrality of national securities legislation be ensured, i.e. that crypto-assets containing rights corresponding to, for example, shares or bonds (investment tokens) are regulated as shares and bonds (investment securities). A legislative solution is now being sought (working discussions started in March, completion hopefully by the end of the year). The Markets in Crypto-assets Regulation (MiCA) will create a new financial services sector with relatively strict rules similar to those in investment services, including market protection. MiCA is a relatively complicated piece of legislation, it is several hundred pages of text, which will be supplemented by several dozen implementing European regulations. Issuers of so-called stablecoins (crypto-assets maintaining a stable value to a certain currency or basket of assets) are the most strictly regulated in MiCA, this part of MiCA was aimed primarily at Facebook's project (Libra/Diem), which has since been terminated, and is unlikely to be very relevant for entrepreneurs in the Czech Republic. Most stablecoins are pegged to the US dollar, a minority to the euro. These are unlikely to be issued in the Czech Republic, and we are not aware of any crown stablecoin. However, the main impacts are likely to be on crypto-asset service providers (i.e. in particular exchange offices and exchanges, the operation of machines for the sale of crypto-assets, as well as consultancy), who will have to be licensed. It will also have a certain impact on the issuance of crypto-assets (white papers - similar to a prospectus). MiCA is now in the final stages of the approval process (currently expected to be published in the Official Journal in June 2023) and is expected to come into force in 2025. Until then, it will be necessary to adopt a large amount of implementing European legislation on MiCA, which addresses the details of the functioning of the proposed rules and which is currently being prepared - the CNB will participate in the creation of dozens of implementing regulations within the ESA. The CNB's priority is to set up the implementing rules appropriately so as to ensure a sufficient level of protection for users and at the same time not to unnecessarily create obstacles to the functioning of crypto-asset services and the issuance of crypto-assets. The CNB holds regular meetings with the FinTech community on specific topics related to financial innovation. In the future, they will certainly also apply to the new MiCA regulation. Entities considering providing cryptoservices must take into account that meeting the MiCA requirements will not be easy and will require intensive preparation for applying for a license as a crypto-asset service provider. On the contrary, MiCA opens up space for the entry of existing financial market participants into the crypto-asset market, as it facilitates the issuance of crypto-assets and the provision of crypto-asset services to already regulated financial institutions (for example, it will be sufficient for credit institutions to notify the supervisory authority).
text_original: Nazen o trzch s kryptoaktivy (MiCA) vytvo nov sektor finannch slueb Jan Prochzka, len bankovn rady NB Konference Efektivn stt - partner kryptoprmyslu Sent Parlamentu esk Republiky Praha, 26. dubna 2023 len bankovn rady NB Jan Prochzka se v Sentu ve stedu 26. dubna zastnil konference Efektivnstt- partner kryptoprmyslu. Ve svm vystoupen hovoil o regulaci kryptoaktiv v R i EU. Vybran citace z vystoupen Jana Prochzky v Sentu Aktuln se na kryptoaktiva, nenapluj-li definici regulovanch finannch slueb, co me bt ppad napklad elektronickch penz i derivt, vztahuj v R pouze pravidla pro pedchzen legalizaci vnos z trestn innosti a dohled Finannho analytickho adu (FA), jinak kryptoaktiva nepodlhaj finann regulaci ani dohledu NB. Investoi by si tto skutenosti mli bt vdomi a zohledovat ve svch investinch rozhodnutch souvisejc rizika, na n NB veejnost prbn upozoruje. NB toto pokldala za dostaten a obecn nepovaovala za potebn kryptoaktiva regulovat jako finann sluby, a nenavrhovala tedy v minulosti dnou speciln nrodn prvn pravu pro kryptoaktiva a innosti s nimi spojen, jak byla zavedena v nkterch lenskch sttech EU. Na rovni EU stle nen harmonizovna prava definice tokenizovanch investinch cennch papr, kter je tak pedmtem vnitrosttn pravy v jednotlivch lenskch sttech. To vede k situaci, e v nkterch zemch EU jsou investin tokeny povaovny za investin cenn papry a podlhaj standardn regulaci finannmu trhu (zejm. MFID2), zatmco v jinch, vetn R, tomu tak nen. Proto NB dlouhodob poaduje zajistit technologickou neutralitu nrodn pravy cennch papr, tedy aby kryptoaktiva obsahujc prva odpovdajc nap. akcim i dluhopism (investin tokeny) byla regulovna jako akcie a dluhopisy (investin cenn papry). Nyn se hled legislativn een (pracovn diskuse byly zahjeny v beznu, dokonen snad do konce roku). Nazen o trzch s kryptoaktivy (MiCA) vytvo nov sektor finannch slueb s relativn psnmi pravidly obdobnmi tm v investinch slubch, vetn ochrany trhu. MiCA je pomrn komplikovan prvn pedpis, jde o nkolik set strnek textu, kter jet bude doplovat nkolik destek provdcch evropskch pedpis. Nejpsnji jsou v MiCA regulovni vydavatel tzv. stablecoins (kryptoaktiv udrujcch stabiln hodnotu k urit mn i koi aktiv), tato st MiCA mila primrn na mezitm ji ukonen projekt spolenosti Facebook (Libra/Diem) a pro podnikatele v R nejspe nebude pli relevantn. Vtina stablecoins je navzna na americk dolar, menina na euro. Ty pravdpodobn nebudou vydvny v R, nejsme si pitom vdomi dnho korunovho stablecoinu. Zsadn dopady ale zejm budou na poskytovatele slueb souvisejcch s kryptoaktivy (tj. zejmna smnrny a burzy, provoz automat pro prodej kryptoaktiv, ale i poradenstv), kte se budou muset licencovat. Urit dopad pak bude mt i na vydvn kryptoaktiv (white papers - obdoba prospektu). MiCA je nyn ve finln fzi schvalovacho procesu (v souasnosti se oekv jej uveejnn v ednm vstnku v ervnu 2023) a jeho innost se oekv v roce 2025. Do t doby bude poteba pijmout i velk mnostv provdc evropsk legislativy k MiCA, kter e detaily fungovn navrench pravidel a kter se v tto chvli pipravuje - NB se v rmci ESA bude astnit tvorby destek provdcch pedpis. Prioritou NB je vhodn nastaven provdcch pravidel tak, abychom zajistili dostatenou mru ochrany pro uivatele a zrove zbyten nevytveli pekky pro fungovn slueb spojench s kryptoaktivy a vydvn kryptoaktiv. NB pod pravideln setkn s FinTech komunitou vnovan konkrtnm tmatm spojenm s finannmi inovacemi. V budoucnu se budou urit tkat i novho nazen MiCA. Subjekty uvaujc o poskytovn kryptoslueb mus potat s tm, e splnn poadavk MiCA nebude jednoduch a z jejich strany bude nutn intenzivn pprava na podn dosti o licenci poskytovatele slueb spojench s kryptoaktivy. Naopak MiCA otevr prostor pro vstup existujcch subjekt finannho trhu na trh s kryptoaktivy, nebo usnaduje vydvn kryptoaktiv a poskytovn slueb s kryptoaktivy ji regulovanm finannm institucm (napklad vrovm institucm bude postaovat oznmen dohledovmu orgnu).

Title: Speech by Jan Prochzka at the CAP conference
text: Speech by Jan Prochazka at the CAP conference Jan Prochazka, CNB Bank Board member Conference of the Czech Insurance Association Prague, 21 November 2023 Ladies and gentlemen, On behalf of myself and the Governor of the Czech National Bank, I would like to welcome you to this conference dedicated to 30 years of development of the modern insurance market in the Czech Republic. The insurance industry can undoubtedly be considered one of the most important sectors of financial services, which in its essence helps citizens and entrepreneurs to protect their property, living situations, health and income from unforeseeable events. In the Czech Republic, the insurance market has undergone significant development in the last 30 years. The basic pillars of the modern insurance market, which created a stable legal framework for the functioning of the insurance market and enabled its development, were set by the Insurance Act and the Civil Code (in the meantime also by the Insurance Contract Act). Over the years, there have been other significant legislative changes, such as the demonopolisation of motor vehicle liability insurance or, from the CNB's point of view, the harmonisation of Czech public law with European law, which has resulted in the current Insurance Act, which implements the new Solvency II prudential supervision framework, or the Insurance and Reinsurance Distribution Act, transposing the IDD Directive. Together with the strong background and know-how of international financial groups and domestic owners and operating on the open market of the European Union, the insurance market in the Czech Republic has become stable, fully competitive, well-capitalised, profitable and sufficiently resistant to potential adverse influences from the CNB's point of view. This was confirmed, among other things, by the 12th round of supervisory stress tests of insurance companies carried out on end-of-2022 data, which took place in the first half of 2023. On behalf of the CNB, I thank you for your participation in it. Nevertheless, I would like to mention some risks and uncertainties, as well as opportunities for the further functioning of this sector.  First of all, there are macroeconomic and geopolitical developments: inflation and high interest rates, the realization or threat of conflicts (Ukraine, Israel, China's expansionist policy, local conflicts in Africa). It is also necessary to mention climate change and its inclusion in the reinsurance market, among other things.  In connection with the occurrence of natural calamities and their imminent future increase due to changes in climatic conditions, as well as in connection with the uncertainties arising from the reverberations of the coronavirus pandemic, insurance companies are at risk of a significant increase in the price of reinsurance in some insurance sectors or its limited availability. This trend has already been partially reflected in the conditions for negotiating reinsurance programmes for 2023. Ultimately, this may cause insurance prices to increase or even adjust product offerings to include or extend exclusions in relation to environmental risks, as well as limit the availability of insurance coverage for certain customer segments or industries. From a long-term point of view, it is necessary to mention an important segment of the insurance market in the Czech Republic, which is third-party liability insurance and its sufficiency of premiums. It is characterized by a highly competitive environment with a standardized, almost commodity product that can be easily sold through web comparison engines. This is causing great pressure on the price, especially for new business, in an environment of significant damage inflation. Although the lower loss frequency caused by fleet modernization, more expensive fuel prices and structural changes caused by the Covid-19 pandemic has so far helped to maintain profitability, it is generally expected to return to at least partial pre-Covid levels, which, together with persistent loss inflation, is expected to worsen the profitability of third-party insurance. I would also like to focus on cyber risks and digitization. There is undoubtedly a higher risk of cyber attacks caused by structural changes in the functioning of insurance companies and their clients (higher share of home office and higher online processes) and at the same time the conflict in Ukraine, where a greater volume of attacks by Russian hackers on EU countries can be observed.[11 The digitization of insurance company processes is growing significantly and it can be assumed that this trend will continue. The development in the implementation of artificial intelligence in the activities of insurance companies is obvious, its more effective involvement appears more in internal processes, e.g. in underwriting risks, including segmentation of those interested in insurance and determining the amount of premiums. In direct contact with the customer, e.g. in the provision of information and in the distribution of insurance, the use of artificial intelligence is rather in its infancy. The introduction of these new technologies places greater demands on the management of risks related to both direct interaction with customers and internal procedures of insurance companies in order to minimize the risk of damage to the interests of customers and also to prevent discrimination against them. From the point of view of the economics of the functioning of the entire insurance market, there is of course a trend of market consolidation, pressure on efficiency and the use of outsourcing. The ongoing consolidation of the Czech insurance market has resulted in a number of acquisitions and mergers in recent years and efforts to increase efficiency (including the search for synergies through operating in some markets through branches). The effort to streamline procedures, reduce costs and use synergies within financial groups is reflected in the outsourcing of a number of activities of insurance companies to external providers and group service companies. We understand this trend, it is a logical tool for sharing costs, but also expertise within the group. However, there is a need for a clear definition of responsibilities at the level of the companies involved and for appropriate quality controls to be set up. The inconsistent approach of some insurance companies increases their exposure to legal and reputational risk. The cost streamlining of activities with the aim of realizing savings in the management of the tribe and reducing the demands on the processes of settling insurance claims is also evident in the form of transferring existing clients to new, currently offered non-life and life insurance products. However, these processes entail the obligation to meet the requirements imposed by the regulation, in particular on transparent communication towards the affected customers (e.g. on changes in the scope of insurance coverage, exclusions, the method of payment of premiums, etc.) and to carry out an analysis of their current requirements and needs under the conditions set by the relevant regulation. And last but not least, there are also legislative changes that affect the everyday life of insurance companies to a greater extent than before. From a prudential point of view, it is also necessary to keep in mind current or upcoming legislative changes, such as the revision of Solvency II, IRRD or the introduction of IFRS 17. From the point of view of professional care and consumer protection, the medium-term challenge for the sector is to cope with the demanding regulation concerning sustainable finance rules (currently, in particular, the process of assessing customers' sustainability preferences in the distribution of investment life insurance and the integration of sustainability into product supervision requirements) and the further reflection of EIOPA's non-legislative activities in the area of product management and consumer protection in general in insurance activities (value for money, bankinsurance, etc.). We are therefore glad that we have been in a long-term dialogue with the market on these issues in order to clarify each other's expectations of regulation and ensure its rational implementation. In conclusion, I would like to express my appreciation for the activities of the Czech Association of Insurance Companies, which will celebrate 30 years of its existence this year, especially in the area of cultivating the insurance market, an integral part of which is the self-regulation of the market through so-called self-regulatory standards. The CNB has a positive view of the existence of a living self-regulatory framework that responds to current stimuli and needs not only on the insurance market. We consider this to be very important and beneficial, especially in the context of those issues that are currently not sufficiently reflected in the requirements of legal regulations and at the same time can be considered essential, especially from the client's point of view. The supervision perceives that the member insurance companies of the CAP usually feel bound by the self-regulatory standards and often refer to them, and this is reflected in the supervision in the assessment of the risk profile of the individual institution. One of the association's most recent activities on the topic of underinsurance, which resonates in the context of climate change and the level of inflation, is, for example, the creation of a calculator of property insurance insured values, which will allow those interested in insurance to obtain a general overview of the value of their real estate under insurance. Although the CNB does not approve self-regulatory standards, we consider it useful to have ongoing mutual communication between the CAP and the CNB in the preparation of some of them, where I believe we have repeatedly contributed our recommendations to the quality of their content. I would also like to express my appreciation for the activities of the Czech Insurers' Bureau, which contributes to the safety and smooth functioning of the third-party liability insurance market with its high-quality data, analytical and professional support to individual insurance companies. I wish not only the association on its birthday, but the entire insurance market to maintain its good condition, performance and reputation in the years to come, which will bring new challenges - some of which we already know about today, and some may be completely new. Just as a person is not only an adult at the age of 30, but also experienced enough to be able to take care of his family and face a number of obstacles, we believe that Czech insurance companies and the entire insurance market, after having undergone many stress tests not only in recent years, have proven that they are able to take care of their clients (sufficiently prudently and with professional care). [1] In the second half of 2022 and early 2023, the second round of ICT risk assessments took place for the six most important insurance companies operating on the Czech insurance market, and other insurance companies will follow this year.

V esk republice proel pojistn trh v poslednch 30 letech vznamnm vvojem. Zkladn pile modernho pojistnho trhu, kter vytvoily stabiln prvn rmec pro fungovn pojistnho trhu a umonily jeho rozvoj, byly nastaveny zkonem o pojiovnictv a obanskm zkonkem (v meziase tak zkonem o pojistn smlouv). I pesto bych rd zmnil nkter rizika a nejistoty, ale i pleitosti pro dal fungovn tohoto sektoru. V prv ad je to makroekonomick a geopolitick vvoj: inflace a vysok rokov sazby, realizace i hrozba konflikt (Ukrajina, Izrael, expanzivn politika ny, lokln konflikty v Africe). Dle je teba zmnit klimatick zmny a jejich propsn mimo jin do zajistnho trhu. V souvislosti s vskytem prodnch kalamit a jejich hrozcm budoucm nrstem z dvodu zmn klimatickch podmnek a zrove v souvislosti s nejistotami vyplvajcmi z dozvuk koronavirov pandemie pojiovnm hroz vznamn zdraen cen zajitn v nkterch pojistnch odvtvch, ppadn jeho omezen dostupnost. Tento trend se sten ji promtl do podmnek pi sjednvn zajistnch program na rok 2023. V konenm dsledku to me zpsobit nrst cen pojitn i dokonce pravu produktov nabdky smujc k zahrnut i rozen vluk ve vztahu k environmentlnm rizikm a tak omezen dostupnosti pojistnho kryt pro nkter segmenty zkaznk nebo odvtv. Z dlouhodobho hlediska je teba zmnit vznamn segment pojistnho trhu v R, kterm je povinn ruen a jeho postaitelnost pojistnho. Vyznauje se vysoce konkurennm prostedm se standardizovanm, tm komoditnm produktem, kter je mon snadno prodvat pes webov srovnvae. To zpsobuje velk tlak na cenu zejmna u novho obchodu, a to v prosted vznamn kodn inflace. Udren ziskovosti sice dosud napomh ni kodn frekvence zpsoben modernizac vozovho parku, dra cenou paliv a strukturlnmi zmnami zpsobenmi pandemi covid-19, nicmn se veobecn oekv jej alespo sten nvrat na pedcovidov hodnoty, co bude dle oekvn spolu s petrvvajc kodn inflac zhorovat profitabilitu povinnho ruen. Dle bych se rd vnoval kybernetickm rizikm a digitalizaci. Bezesporu zde existuje vy riziko kybernetickch tok zpsoben strukturlnmi zmnami fungovn pojioven a jejich klient (vy podl home Office a vy mra online proces) a zrove konfliktem na Ukrajin, kdy lze pozorovat vt objem tok ruskch hacker na zem EU.[11 Digitalizace proces pojioven vznamn narst a lze pedpokldat, e tento trend bude pokraovat. Rozvoj v oblasti implementace uml inteligence do innost pojioven je zejm, jej efektivnj zapojen se jev spe v internch procesech, nap. pi upisovn rizik vetn segmentace zjemc o pojitn a stanovovn ve pojistnho. V pmm kontaktu se zkaznkem, nap. pi poskytovn informac a pi distribuci pojitn, je vyuit uml inteligence spe v potcch. Zavdn tchto novch technologi klade vy nroky na zen rizik souvisejcch jak s pmou interakc se zkaznky, tak s vnitnmi postupy pojioven, aby bylo minimalizovno riziko pokozen zjm zkaznk a tak nedochzelo k jejich diskriminaci. Title: Global Dialogue on Regulatory Approaches for Inclusive FinTech Closing statement at the conference Prague
Subtitle: Regulatory Approaches for Inclusive Fintech
text: 27. 9. 2019 Dedek Oldrich Regulatory Approaches for Inclusive Fintech Oldrich Dedek, CNB Board Member Global Dialogue on Regulatory Approaches for Inclusive FinTech Closing statement at the conference Prague, 27th September 2019 Ladies and Gentlemen. I would like to thank you for attending this conference for which the Czech National Bank gladly provided this Congress Centre. All speakers also deserve my thanks. I am convinced that the discussion was rich and thought-provoking and contributed to further understanding of the topics discussed. This conference addressed the issues of financial inclusion. To be frank, when I joined the Bank Board, I hardly knew what this term meant. But after attending a few FinTech events, my knowledge improved. I realised and appreciated the goals of financial inclusion in terms of providing diverse social groups, namely in less developed countries, with access to financial products at a reasonable price. The connection with FinTech innovations is also straightforward. Even in the less developed world, these diverse social groups own mobile phones and have access to the Internet. One might conclude from that that the key goals of financial inclusion are not so relevant for advanced economies with a well- developed, stable and competitive banking sector. But financial inclusion covers a larger agenda, crucial for advanced economies as well. One of the interesting areas is connected with the phenomenon of Big Data, gathered through social media and other channels in which people leave a digital footprint. As a result, financial institutions could get better evaluation of client risks and based on this knowledge, they could even exclude some customers from using certain risky financial instruments. Regarding the distinction between less and more advanced countries, I need to stress the following point. It happens to us in the European Union that we are so focused on the implementation of our Europe-wide initiatives, such as PSD2 or GDPR, that we cease paying adequate attention to achievements elsewhere. At the same time, the developing countries advantage is that while catching up they can leapfrog the current business models or technologies that are slowly becoming obsolete and thus reach the cutting edge earlier than us. That's why frank exchange of views, such as weve had over the last two days, is valuable for us at the Czech central bank, and we are very glad that we could provide space for it to take place. I would like to point out in this regard particularly the discussions on Creating and Enabling FinTech Ecosystems and on cybersecurity frameworks and their implementation by various central banks. Ladies and gentlemen. We live in an increasingly digitalized world which poses new challenges to central banks as well. One of them is CBDC which stands for Central Bank Digital Currency. It's a hot issue, for example, in Sweden, where the volume of cash in circulation is permanently falling in absolute terms and smart phones have become the main payment instrument. So far it is not a prevailing trend as witnessed in the Czech Republic, where the volume of currency in circulation is continuously rising and we have to invest large amounts of money in purchasing and maintaining machines for controlling the quality of and sorting banknotes and coins. There are a lot of unanswered questions regarding CBDC. For example:  Should central banks compete with private money administered by commercial banks? The banks invest massively in user- friendly and service-rich internet banking. So the question is whether the Czech National Bank should also invest in these systems in order to keep up with the commercial banking sector.  Another concern is what would be the motives of the general public in using CBDC? Is it because a central bank cannot, by definition, go bankrupt? However, this has its own risks, namely a run on the banking sector or flight to safe central bank money in turbulent times.  Last but not least, this issue also raises questions in terms of costs for the central bank budget. How many new employees should we hire to be in contact with a nation-wide clientele? As I said earlier, there are more questions than answers. Let me mention one more fresh, new challenge, posed by the emergence of so-called Global Stable Coins. As you now, Facebook has a plan to create a currency that millions of people all around the world would use. Let me remind you that central banks are the outcome of evolutionary recognition that monetary authorities cannot by guided by profit-making. Why? Because it would be easy for central banks to earn money through highly selfish behaviour. They might be tempted to push inflation up because higher inflation increases demand for banknotes, which are a source of seignorage. Another temptation might be to permanently depreciate domestic currency in order to reap accounting profits. Facebook and other social media are private bodies, guided by the profit principle. Some of them have the ambition to issue money of their own. On the one hand, we cannot stop progress. On the other hand, we should not repeat the bumpy evolution from private money to modern central banking. Let me conclude with the obvious fact that the entire financial world has been changing, meaning central banks must be able to cope with this changing environment, characterized by the influx of FinTech innovations. More importantly, how active and supportive should central banks be in this area? According to standard classification, the options are becoming a contact point, an innovation hub or a sandbox. For now, the Czech National Bank has decided not to take the most demanding route, the sandbox. It would mean amending some laws and the application of double standards for regulated entities. The CNB is responsible for supervising the entire financial sector, so we have a host of problems to be solved even without the FinTech industry. We have to weigh the pros and cons of alternative uses of human and financial resources thoroughly. We don't yet know what the actual demand for this central bank service will be. So, we think that it is a good decision to start by creating a platform through which we will help FinTech companies by clarifying the existing regulation and by organizing an exchange of views. Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for your attention. I wish you a safe flight to your final destinations.

Title: Meeting of the Central Bank Governance Network Bank of Thailand Bangkok
Subtitle: Remarks by Marek Mora at the special session on central bank openness
text: 21.9. Mora 2018 Marek Remarks by Marek Mora at the special session on central bank openness Marek Mora, CNB Board member Meeting of the Central Bank Governance Network Bank of Thailand Bangkok, 20th - 21st September 2018 Ladies and gentlemen, dear colleagues, It is a pleasure and honour for me to be given the opportunity to wrap up our todays session on openness. Many important issues have been raised from various perspectives. Before starting let me just mention two things. First, I would like to thank David Archer for organising this network. Since joining the Czech National Bank one and a half years ago, I have thought on several occasions that we were reinventing the wheel when we were trying to find solutions to some of our problems. And this meeting has confirmed this suspicion of mine and also gave me a guide on where to look for the answers. And second, let me use this opportunity to thank the Bank of Thailand for amazing organisation and hospitality. Origins of openness in central banking Obviously, openness - its understanding, the way it is conducted and practiced, the channels which are used or considered to be most effective - all that very much depends on the history and tradition of each central bank and on the country and culture in which the central bank operates. There is obviously not a single recipe for the best universal approach to openness. Openness in central banking has been historically linked mainly to its core and most traditional business, i.e. to monetary policy. It was important for central banks to be understood primarily by the markets in order to make the monetary policy transmission mechanism more effective. This logic applies even more to those central banks with an inflation targeting regime, in which open communication of the central bank is a key factor of success and has become a policy instrument. This is a difference from monetary policy practice in the past, say 20-25 years ago, when many central bankers believed that monetary policy decisions should take the markets by surprise in order to achieve maximum impact. There are several theoretical and many empirical studies showing that trust in a central bank has a significantimpact on inflation expectations. And trust is in turn very much dependent on knowledge people have about the central bank. Therefore, steering inflation expectations through central bank communication and trust-building (which both depend on openness) seems promising. Why is openness so high on central banks agenda NOW? The need for openness has increased over time. In my view, there are several reasons for that. First, we have just celebrated the tenth anniversary ofLehman Brothers. This and the consequent events have changed the public perception of banking and bankers. And the change was obviously negative. Bankers have been seen as greedy, irresponsible people who not only caused the most severe recent economic crisis, but on top of that who have not suffered themselves from this crisis (and who even gained in this crisis). This Lehman Brother effect applies in my view also to central banks. The crisis produced general distrust and suspicion, also about central banks, and more openness is seen as an instrument to regain trust! Second, in the area of monetary policy, the financial crisis forced many central banks to useunconventional instruments. These instruments sometime produce complicated side effects. In particular, it turns out to be very difficult to explain to the public why price stability should be more important than any other policy objective (for instance the central banks loss or exchange rate stability), and why inflation should be positive (for instance 2% per year). And why not zero? And why couldnt it be negative? The unconventional monetary policies also have major redistributive effects. There was a need to explain them in public, sometimes to defend oneself. Third, many central banks have been given additional competencies over time. The Czech National Bank is a very good example. We are not only a monetary authority responsible for price stability, payment systems and cash circulation We are also responsible for the supervision over the whole Czech financial system (i.e. not only for banks), forfinancial stability, and for consumer protection. We are also the nationalbank resolution authority. We have several mandates, some of them could be even considered contradictory. All that means that the need - not only among experts, but also among politicians and the broader public - to understand our policies has increased. And our duty is to explain all these policies. So, multiple mandates of the central bank increase the need to communicate and make the communication more complex. Fourth, we are living in anew environment. There have been dramatic developments in information and communication technology and also new information laws have increased public access to what was previously private. As a result, all other actors are communicating, almost on a permanent basis. These new developments do not make it even possible for a public institution like a central bank not to communicate. And last but not least, and more generally, I would also consider the requirements for openness as a counterbalance to central bank independence. Greater openness and transparency are a tool for greater accountability and legitimacy. What are the main trends among central banks towards openness? Almost all central banks continue using their traditional way ofcommunication via reporting to their national parliaments and by publishing their main information and reports. However, these ways of communication are nowadays not enough - for reasons mentioned above, but in some countries also for a lack of parliamentarians' interest and understanding of the central banks functions. There could be other ways of benefiting from openness. For instance, the Czech National Bank opened itself to an audit of its accounts by the Czech Supreme Audit Office. The findings of the Office have been very positive, among the best (if not the best) among Czech public institutions. This information was published and it also contributed to a better public reputation of the CNB. Central banks explore more direct communication channels. There has also clearly been a shift in the communication target group: from analysts and financial markets to a broader public. The aim is to get across to everyone (the bottom of the pyramid). The ways to do it are:  Use simple, short, understandable, jargon-free language  Communicate in a more targeted way (the one-size-fits-all approach does not work)  Where appropriate, pictures could tell more than words  The messages should be cascaded, put in layers in terms of detail (layer 1 the just the decision, layer 2 the decision and a bit of explanation, layer 3 the decision and a broader background)  Communication and openness is a two-way street, it also includes feedback; an active strategy seems to work better than a re-active/defensive strategy (not everything should be corrected, we should simply continue telling our story to the public) The means used for such direct communication range from very virtual ones (social media such as Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, Linkedln) to very physical and tangible ones (open days, visiting centres, visits of senior representatives at schools and regions etc.). Importantly, openness is not only communication. It could be also about the central bank making sure that the broader public perceives the central bank as doing the right job. For instance by securing access for everyone in less developed countries to an account and thus to credit. Financial education could be important for perceived openness. External openness and communication also have an impact on the internal functioning of central banks. It affects organisational structures and working habits. It seems that monetary policy departments (especially in central banks using inflation targeting) are more at ease with openness than some other departments. There is an issue of internal communication. Being more open towards the broader public also forces central banks to be shorter and punchier in their internal communication. Those central banks seem to be more successful in openness when they are supported by top management. That also sends an important message to the staff. And also, it makes a difference if the communication department comes in early in the production chain. But one should always keep in mind the question of effectiveness of central bank communication. How much did more openness contribute to better public perception? How do we measure it? Possible limits to openness The debate during the meetings has also shown that there are limits to openness. For instance, many central banks are involved in areas where they cannot reveal information because of legal limits to openness and because of professional secrecy. There are also arguments that in monetary policy too much openness could be less than optimal The argument is that central banks could give the impression that they know more than they do. There could be a risk if private agents rely too much on the wisdom of central banks. This argument has been brought forward by Lustenberger and Rossi (2017).! There also seems to be a trade-off between gaining a broader audience by simpler communication and losing the experts. More is not always better! People perceive central banks as powerful and secretive on the one hand, but successful, responsible, professional and efficient on the other hand. Arent these just two sides of the same coin? Conclusion To conclude, openness has been high on the agenda of central bankers. This morning we have heard many invaluable comments on this issue. My main take-away from the session this morning is that more openness and better communication are very important for central banks. But communication should not be a substitute for good policy If central banks fail to maintain price and financial stability, even the fanciest communication using Facebook and Instagram wont save it! Thank you for your attention! Mellina, S., and T. Schmidt (2018), The Role of Central Bank Knowledge and Trust for the Publics Inflation Expectations, Deutsche Bundesbank Discussion Paper 32/2018. Lustenberger, T., and E. Rossi (2017), Does Central Bank Transparency and Communication Affect Financial and Macroeconomic Forecasts?, SNB Working Papers 12/2017.

Title: Speech by Governor Jan Rusnok at the presentation of the commemorative banknote Karel Engli
text: Ales Michl: The current level of inflation still makes it impossible to lower interest rates Ales Michl, CNB Govemor Senate of the Czech Republic Prague, 27 July 2023 During the discussion of the Financial Market Supervision Report for 2022 in the Senate of the Czech Republic, CNB Governor Ales Michl delivered a speech on the current fight against inflation, the liquidation of Sberbank and the CNBs financial results. President, esteemed senators, good afternoon, I am honoured to be here with you today. One year ago, in July 2022, the new CNB Bank Board took over responsibility for the monetary policy and financial stability of our country. The situation at the time was as follows: First, we had the highest inflation in history, leaving aside the price growth that occurred during the countrys economic transition in the early nineties. Second, during the liquidation of Sberbank, lawsuits were brought challenging the liquidation process. These lawsuits were brought both by representatives of private firms and by representatives of regions, cities and municipalities. Helping to ensure the transparency of the process of liquidating Sberbank was important for us in terms of financial stability and credibility. And third, we took up the reins of the CNB at a time when it had posted its largest loss and the worst financial results in its history. We have started to deal with all of these problems. Les first look at how we reduced inflation: We opted for a strategy of keeping interest rates unchanged at 7%. Interest rates were at their highest level in more than 20 years and were already sufficiently dampening economic activity. Key to our strategy was that we supplemented it with a strong koruna policy. The koruna was at its strongest level ever in spring of this year if you take the monthly average for April 2023. The stabilisation of interest rates together with the strong koruna meant we had the tightest monetary conditions in 25 years. I am therefore now able to communicate to you the results of our work so far: Inflation has started to come down gradually from 18% in September. Inflation is now already just below 10%. But it is still not at a level we would be happy with. Inflation is still high. It is at a level which still makes it impossible to lower interest rates. This level of inflation requires us to adopt a hawkish policy Stance. It is necessary to ensure that inflation does not remain persistent and decreases further. As regards the second problem, it was important for financial stability for us to become active members of the creditors committee in the process of liquidating Sberbank. Together with the insolvency trustee Ms Jiina Luzova, we managed to set up the entire process properly. We also managed to get everyone on board, even those who were initially challenging the process. Representatives of firms, regions, cities and municipalities withdrew their lawsuits. A large proportion of Sberbanks assets sold very well. eska spoitelna bought Sberbanks mortgage portfolios. Part of its other assets was also sold. The assets which remain are those subject to sanctions. I have good news for the public and representatives of regions and cities: I expect the insolvency trustee to introduce a pian soon for the payout of the remaining part of the assets not previously covered by the Guarantee Fund. Arecovery rate of 100% is very likely. A large share of the money should be paid out this year, and the rest next year. If that is the ase, it will be very positive news. In addition, we inherited the CNBs largest-ever accounting loss. This will be dealt with over a number of years, as it cannot be resolved immediately. This problem does not prevent us from fighting inflation. It does not prevent us from fulfilling our mandate. But it is a problem for the future and I do not want to hand the bank over to the next governor with another large accounting loss. The problem boils down to our balance sheet comprising assets with an expected annual return of 2-3%. On the liabilities side, we have a large amount of koruna we now have to remunerate at 7%. The excess koruna was generated above all in lat 2016 and early 2017, when the central bank made perhaps the biggest economic policy mistake - a huge quantity of money was created to weaken the koruna and increase inflation. We must now withdraw this money and remunerate it to prevent it from fuelling further inflation. That is the main reason we have posted a loss. And until we tame inflation, we will probably continue to make a loss. However, we are dealing with the problem and will resolve it. Thank you for listening to my opening remarks. Deputy Governor Jan Frait and I are now ready to answer any questions you might have.

Title: Speech by the CNB Governor on the occasion of the ceremonial presentation of the Mikulov gold coin
text: Speech by the CNB Governor on the occasion of the ceremonial presentation of the gold coin issue Mikulov Jii Rusnok, CNB Governor Mikulov, 31 May 2022 Dear Ladies and Gentlemen, Dear Guests, It is my pleasant duty to welcome you all to the Mikulov Castle on the occasion of the presentation of the gold coin "Mikulov Urban Monument Reserve". The coin is issued by the Czech National Bank in the number of 13 thousand pieces and is the third coin in a series of ten gold coins dedicated to urban heritage reserves. In my speech, I will primarily focus on the introduction of the new gold coin. The journey from the competition through production to its current issue took more than a year and a half. Already in November 2020, we announced a competition, or prizes for the submission of an artistic design of this gold coin. 13 artists submitted and submitted their artistic designs. The evaluation of the designs - specifically the plaster models - was carried out on 16 February 2021 by the Commission for the Evaluation of Designs for Czech Banknotes and Coins under the chairmanship of JUDr. The Deputy Mayor of Mikulov, Sylva Chludilova, participated in the evaluation of the proposals. The final decision was made by the CNB Bank Board in April 2021, when it confirmed the Commission's decision and approved the realisation of the coin designed by the sculptor Zbynk Fojt. The coins were then minted at the Czech Mint in Jablonec nad Nisou, a total of 13,000 coins, of which 4,100 were of normal quality and 8,900 were of top quality. These variants differ in surface treatment. Top quality coins have a highly polished coin field and a smooth edge. Coins in normal quality have a milled edge of the coin. About 200 kilograms of pure gold were used to produce 13,000 gold coins, which represents 16 gold bars, if you want gold bars (1 bar weighs about 12.5 kg). For those interested, I will mention a few technical details: the coin weighs 15.55 grams, has a diameter of 28 millimeters and the thickness of the coin is 1.85 millimeters. And now let me focus on the form of the gold coin designed by Zbynk Fojt. The left obverse side of the coin depicts Mikulov Castle, in the middle of the coin is a composition of stylised heraldic animals and provincial coats-of-arms, i.e. the Czech lion at the top, the Moravian eagle in the middle and the Silesian eagle at the bottom. To the right of the heraldic animals is the vertical inscription Czech Republic. The right-hand side of the obverse side of the coin also depicts a statue of Pomona from the medieval fountain in the square. The denomination of the CZK 5000 coin is located above the Czech Ivo. The text "Mstske pamatkove rezervace", i.e. the name of the cycle of gold coins, is written around the right-hand edge of the coin. On the obverse side, above the roof of the Mikulov chateau, there is also the manufacturer's mark - the Czech Mint. The reverse side of the coin depicts important architectural monuments, from the left is the Dietrichstein Tomb, the Upper Synagogue and the sgraffito burgher house U Ryti. At the top there is a horizontal text "City" and a vertical text "Mikulov". The year of mintage is located above the depiction of the Dietrichstein Tomb and finally the initials of the designer of the coin Zbynk Fojt are located near the right-hand edge of the reverse side of the coin. The nominal value of the coin is CZK 5000, but the selling price is higher and takes into account the current price of gold and the costs associated with the production of the coin. Regular sales of commemorative coins of the Czech National Bank are only possible through contractual partners authorised to trade in numismatic material. However, guests of today's presentation can buy the coin today on site. In conclusion, I would like to emphasize that in our Czechoslovak and Czech history, coins and banknotes have been made according to the designs of the best sculptors, medal makers and artists. I believe that the Mikulov gold coin will become one of our most beautiful commemorative coins, that it will gain interest not only among collectors and, last but not least, that it will contribute to the promotion of the beautiful town of Mikulov and its urban conservation area. Thank you for your attention.
text_original: Projev guvernra NB pi pleitosti slavnostn prezentace emise zlat mince Mikulov Ji Rusnok, guvernr NB Mikulov, 31. kvtna 2022 Ven dmy, ven pnov, ven host, je mou milou povinnost Vs vechny pivtat na mikulovskm zmku pi pleitosti prezentace zlat mince Mstsk pamtkov rezervace Mikulov. Vpravo od heraldickch zvat je umstn svisl npis esk republika. Dle pak v prav sti lcn strany mince je zobrazena socha Pomony ze stedovk kany na nmst. Oznaen nominln hodnoty mince 5000 K se nachz nad eskm Ivem. Pi pravm okraji mince je v opisu text Mstsk pamtkov rezervace, tj. nzev cyklu zlatch minc. Ronk raby se nachz nad zobrazenm Dietrichsteinsk hrobky a konen inicily autora mince Zbyka Fojt jsou umstny pi pravm okraji rubov strany mince. Vm, e zlat mince Mikulov se zaad mezi nae nejkrsnj pamtn mince, e si zsk zjem nejen mezi sbrateli a e v neposledn ad pispje k propagaci krsnho msta Mikulov a jeho mstsk pamtkov rezervace. Title: Speech by the CNB Governor on the occasion of the ceremonial presentation of the Jawa 250 silver coin
text: Speech by the CNB Governor on the occasion of the ceremonial presentation of the Jawa 250 silver coin Jii Rusnok, CNB Governor Tynec nad Sazavou, 15 June 2022 Dear Ladies and Gentlemen, Dear Guests, I would like to welcome you here to the JAWA Museum in Tynec nad Sazavou for the ceremonial presentation of a unique silver coin dedicated to the legendary Jawa 250 motorcycle. This is the second coin in the series "Famous means of transport". So far, the Czech National Bank or its predecessor, the State Bank of Czechoslovakia, has not issued a commemorative coin dedicated solely to motorcycles. So today is the first time. This motorcycle, popularly known as the "Kyvacka", was developed in Jawa, then produced and exported to more than 120 countries in 1954-1962. A total of 1.5 million motorcycles sold spread the good name of Czechoslovak industry and engineering in the world, as well as, for example, the sporting achievements of the famous Jawa factory rider Frantisek sastny. I will leave space for further introduction to the Jawa phenomenon to the other speakers and now I would like to try to turn your attention directly to the silver coin with enamelling presented today. The journey to issue the coin took a year and three months. In March 2021, the Czech National Bank announced a competition for the submission of an artistic design for this coin. 13 artists entered the competition and submitted 22 plaster models with a diameter of 190-200 mm. The designs were evaluated by the Commission for the Evaluation of Designs for Czech Banknotes and Coins under the chairmanship of Jaroslav Moravec, with Frantisek Hruska, Executive Director of JAWA Moto, as expert advisor. The CNB Bank Board then selected Petra Brodska's proposal for implementation. The coins were minted by the Czech Mint in Jablonec nad Nisou in the number of 30,000 pieces, of which 20,123 are of top quality, i.e. the field of the coin is highly polished and has a matt relief with a plain edge and the inscription "CNB * Motorcycle * Kyvaka", unlike the normal quality coin, which has a milled edge. The coin was minted from an alloy containing 925 parts silver and 75 parts copper, the diameter of the coin is 40 mm, the weight is 25 g and the thickness is 2.6 mm. The obverse side of the coin depicts three views of parts of a Jawa 250 motorcycle with the inserted divided text "Czech Republic", the denomination "500 K" and the mark of the Czech Mint. The reverse side of the coin depicts an overall view of the motorcycle and two fragments from the technical drawings of the motorcycle. The reverse features the texts "JAWA 250", the year of issuance "2022" and the initials of the designer of the coin, Petra Brodska. The uniqueness of the coin is ensured by the use of red and black synthetic enamel on its reverse side, which reflects the authentic colour scheme of the motorcycle. Enamelling was done by hand with two-component synthetic enamels. The painted parts of the motorcycle are coated with dark red enamel and the typically black parts with black enamel. Other parts of the motorcycle were left in the silver color of the bullion. The applied enamels were hardened for approximately 90 minutes at a temperature of 80 C. The enamelling of the 30,000 pieces produced represented 4,500 hours of work by the most skilled workers and consumed a total of 5 kg of enamels, divided into many thousands of batches, of which only about 1.5 kg of net weight ended up on coins. The nominal price of a coin of 500 crowns is of course not the selling price, it melts higher and takes into account the current price of silver and the costs associated with production. The sale of coins is ensured by contractual partners authorized to trade in numismatic material. Guests of today's presentation can buy the coin today on site. So let's wish the silver coin issued today to become a sought-after collector's item and thus contribute to the even greater popularity of the iconic Jawa 250 motorcycle, because every Czech biker, as is well known, started riding a Jawa. Fans of transport technology can look forward to another silver commemorative coin of the Czech National Bank next year (in June 2023), which will be dedicated to the famous Tatra 603 car. Thank you for your attention.
